---

## Why Do We Turn Pale (or Green) When We're Sick?

### 1. 🩸 Reduced Blood Flow to the Skin (Pallor)

The main reason we look pale when sick is **vasoconstriction** — the narrowing of blood vessels. Vasoconstriction is the narrowing of the blood vessels resulting from contraction of the muscular wall of the vessels, particularly the large arteries and small arterioles. When blood vessels constrict, the flow of blood is restricted or decreased — this makes the skin turn paler because less blood reaches the surface.

Our blood is bright red when oxygenated, and it's a big reason our skin normally has a pinkish hue. When we get nauseous, there's not a lot of blood going to our heads — resulting in that dizzy feeling — and that's why we look pale too, as our oxygenated blood being red is a big reason why our skin is pinkish.

### 2. 🧠 The Nervous System's Role

This pallor isn't random — it's actually driven by your nervous system. Studies show an increase in skin pallor, as revealed by a decrease in the degree of red tone in the skin, with the development of moderate nausea — implying increased **sympathetic nervous system vasoconstriction** of the superficial facial blood vessels.

A physical or psychological event can prompt an immediate sympathetic response that causes cutaneous vasoconstriction, which may turn a patient "white as a ghost." Such hormones can cause cutaneous vasoconstriction and secretion of cold sweat from eccrine glands — which is why we also feel cold and clammy when sick or nauseated.

### 3. 🔄 Blood Being Redirected

The body redirects blood to an affected area of illness, which lowers the effective blood pressure and results in a person appearing pale. Blood flow from all the body is directed and increased to the gastrointestinal system because when we feel nauseated, our body is trying to figure out what is wrong — either to fix it or throw it out by vomiting. This leaves less blood available for the skin, making you look washed out.

### 4. 💧 Dehydration Makes It Worse

When you are "sick," you often become a little dehydrated, which can also contribute to pallor. Dehydration reduces blood volume, compounding the effect of vasoconstriction on your skin color.

### 5. 🟢 The "Green" Part — Is It Real?

Scientifically speaking, the green tinge is subtle, not cartoonish. Not too many people turn truly green — it's mostly a paleness mixed with clamminess. However, research confirms it's real: within one hour of the activation of an innate immune response, there are clear changes in skin coloration — facial skin becomes lighter and less red, while arm skin becomes darker, less red, and less yellow.

The "green" appearance is partly a result of the loss of the red/pink tones in the skin revealing the underlying yellowish-green tones of the skin's natural pigmentation.

### 6. 👁️ Our Brains Are Wired to Notice It

We are exceptional at detecting whether or not people are feeling sick based on their faces — which makes sense, since being around sick people gets you sick; the best way to avoid being sick is to avoid sick people. Maximum color changes occur around the same time as cytokine production and self-reported sickness, but ahead of maximum changes in body temperature and blood pressure. In other words, our bodies visually signal illness very early — before even a fever sets in!

---

**In summary:** Turning pale when sick is primarily your body's nervous system redirecting blood away from the skin to more critical areas (like the gut during nausea). The loss of that rosy, red-oxygenated-blood color in the skin makes you look pale or even slightly greenish, and it's a visible cue that evolution has wired us to recognize and respond to.
